tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

Its first sentence is the sidebar status. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

content.text:
No blockers. Both suites pass: `zig build test` on 0.17.0, and on 0.16.0 with `--cache-dir .zig-cache16`. I also ran `zig fmt --check` with 0.16 on a clean LF copy from `git archive HEAD`, so the CI lint gate passes. The about 80 files a plain local fmt run flags are the Windows checkout's CRLF line endings, not this diff.

**Findings, most important first**

1. **should-fix**, `src/array/array_data.zig:380` (`childCoversRange`, now called from the struct arm at :576). The check compares `child.offset + child.length` with `parent.offset + parent.length`, which mixes the child's and the parent's coordinates. It lets through children that `ArrayRef.slice` and `StructArray.field` then index past their end: for example parent offset 5, length 5, with child offset 8, length 3. `ArrayData.slice` (`array_data.zig:152`) only has debug asserts, so a crafted FFI struct can still read out of bounds in ReleaseFast. The commit's "checked at the trust boundary" claim is therefore not yet true. This hole existed before the diff; it is not a regression. Fix: use the same rule the accessors use, `child.length == parent.length or child.length >= parent.offset + parent.length`. Every struct the library produces satisfies it (builder, slice, IPC, concat, FFI spec form, c_stream export).
2. **should-fix**, same line. No test covers the new struct-coverage rejection. Fix: add one `validateLayout` test with a too-short child that expects `error.InvalidChildren`, plus one row-aligned child that must pass.
3. **should-fix**, `src/ipc/stream_reader.zig:145` and `:320`. The `reader.buffer.ptr == source.data.ptr` precondition is only a debug assert. In release builds a mismatched reader silently gives wrong body bytes. It stays memory-safe because `SharedBuffer.slice` bounds-checks in all modes, but the data is garbage. Fix: add `self.reader.buffer.ptr == self.source.?.data.ptr` to the zero-copy condition at :320 so a mismatch falls back to the copy path.
4. **nit**, `stream_reader.zig:145`. The assert's `seek == 0` clause is unnecessary: `seek` is absolute in a `fixed` reader, so a reader positioned after a prefix (such as the 8-byte Arrow file magic) works fine but trips the assert. Fix: drop that clause.
5. **nit**, `stream_reader.zig` test at :387-441. The test leaks on its error paths. `source` is released by hand after the block, so any `try` inside the block leaks it. `first` also leaks if the second `nextRecordBatch` check fails, and `owned` has no `errdefer` before `toShared`. Fix: `errdefer source.release()` before the block, and `errdefer first.deinit()` inside it.
6. **nit**, `src/concat_array_refs.zig` test (`parts` loop). If a `slice` fails partway through, the parts already made leak, because the `defer` is registered after the loop. Fix: track a filled count, or this can be accepted since it only happens on OOM.
7. **nit**, `src/array/struct_array.zig:84`. The `StructArray.field` change is not isolated by the new test, because there parent and child offsets are equal and the old code also passed. It only matters when a struct's children were already slices with an offset before the struct itself was sliced. Fix: in the double-slice test, build the child from `ib_ref.slice(2, 10)`.
8. **nit**, `src/buffer.zig:226`. Finished arrays now keep up to twice their logical size alive: `toShared` stores the full capacity in the storage and only views `[0..used]`. `len()` is still exact everywhere. I audited every `toShared` caller and all pass a used length, so the IPC writer, FFI export, concat and equality are unaffected. Fix: document it, or shrink in `toShared` when capacity is more than twice `used`.
9. **nit**, `struct_array.zig:1250`. The "builder drops validity after finishReset" test exercises `PrimitiveBuilder` but lives in the struct file. Fix: move it to `primitive_array.zig`.
10. **nit**, `stream_reader.zig:1257`. The comment still says "RecordBatch.init succeeded" but the call is now `initPrevalidated`. Fix: update the comment.

**Checked and clean**
- **Validity drop:** consumers already handle an empty validity buffer, since first batches with no nulls produced one before. `null_count` stays consistent.
- **`initPrevalidated`:** safe, because `readArrayFromMeta` validates every array.
- **`setColumnByName`:** keeps first-match semantics for duplicate names (`getOrPut` keeps the first).
- **Pairwise concat:** sound. Every type path handles `left.offset` symmetrically, the odd trailing ref keeps its order, and the result is always a fresh array.
- **Geometric growth:** `realloc` keeps the 64-byte alignment, and the empty static storage is never freed.
- **Zero-copy:** `canReuseBodySlice` handles alignment, and non-owning sources are copied.
- **Compat:** the three build.zig helpers, the CI matrix, README/CONTRIBUTING and the zon all agree.
- **Over-engineering:** nothing to delete.

**Verdict**
- Mergeable as-is: no blockers, and both compilers pass the full suite.
- Before merge, I'd do findings 1 and 2 (a one-line rule change plus one test), so the trust-boundary claim in the commit message holds.
- Finding 3 is a one-condition change and worth doing in the same commit.
- The nits can follow.

result: zarrow `51a7ca9..HEAD` pre-merge review found no blockers; 3 should-fixes (struct child coverage rule in `array_data.zig:380`, a test for it, release-mode zero-copy reader check in `stream_reader.zig:320`) and 7 nits; tests pass on Zig 0.16.0 and 0.17.0.

No blockers. Both suites pass: `zig build test` on 0.17.0, and on 0.16.0 with `--cache-dir .zig-cache16`. I also ran `zig fmt --check` with 0.16 on a clean LF copy from `git archive HEAD`, so the CI lint gate passes. The ~80 files a plain local fmt run flags are the Windows checkout's CRLF line endings, not this diff.

Findings, most important first:
1. should-fix, src/array/array_data.zig:380 (`childCoversRange`, now called from the struct arm at :576). It compares `child.offset+child.length` with `parent.offset+parent.length`, mixing the child's and parent's coordinates, so it lets through children that ArrayRef.slice and StructArray.field then index past their end (e.g. parent off 5 len 5, child off 8 len 3). ArrayData.slice (array_data.zig:152) has debug asserts only, so a crafted FFI struct can still read out of bounds in ReleaseFast, and the commit's "checked at the trust boundary" claim is not yet true. This hole pre-dates the diff; not a regression. Fix: use the accessors' rule, `child.length == parent.length or child.length >= parent.offset + parent.length`. Every struct the library produces satisfies it (builder, slice, IPC, concat, FFI spec form, c_stream export).
2. should-fix, same line. No test covers the new struct-coverage rejection. Fix: one validateLayout test with a too-short child expecting error.InvalidChildren, plus one row-aligned child that must pass.
3. should-fix, src/ipc/stream_reader.zig:145 and :320. The `reader.buffer.ptr == source.data.ptr` precondition is a debug assert only; in release a mismatched reader silently gives wrong body bytes. Memory-safe (SharedBuffer.slice bounds-checks in all modes), but garbage data. Fix: add `self.reader.buffer.ptr == self.source.?.data.ptr` to the zero-copy condition at :320 so a mismatch falls back to the copy path.
4. nit, stream_reader.zig:145. The assert's `seek == 0` clause is unnecessary: seek is absolute in a fixed reader, so a reader positioned after a prefix (e.g. the 8-byte Arrow file magic) works but trips the assert. Fix: drop the clause.
5. nit, stream_reader.zig test at :387-441 leaks on error paths: `source` is released by hand after the block (any `try` inside leaks it), `first` leaks if the second nextRecordBatch check fails, and `owned` has no errdefer before toShared. Fix: `errdefer source.release()` before the block and `errdefer first.deinit()` inside it.
6. nit, concat_array_refs.zig test (`parts` loop). If a slice fails partway, earlier parts leak because the defer is registered after the loop. Fix: track a filled count, or accept it (OOM only).
7. nit, struct_array.zig:84. The StructArray.field change is not isolated by the new test: there parent and child offsets are equal, so the old code also passed. It only matters when a struct's children were already slices with an offset before the struct was sliced. Fix: build the double-slice test's child from `ib_ref.slice(2, 10)`.
8. nit, buffer.zig:226. Finished arrays now keep up to 2x their logical size alive: toShared stores the full capacity and views [0..used]. len() is still exact everywhere (audited every toShared caller; all pass a used length, so the IPC writer, FFI export, concat and equality are unaffected). Fix: document it, or shrink in toShared when capacity > 2*used.
9. nit, struct_array.zig:1250. The "builder drops validity after finishReset" test exercises PrimitiveBuilder but lives in the struct file. Fix: move it to primitive_array.zig.
10. nit, stream_reader.zig:1257. Comment still says "RecordBatch.init succeeded"; the call is now initPrevalidated. Fix: update the comment.

Checked and clean:
- Validity drop: consumers already handle an empty validity buffer (first batches with no nulls produced one before); null_count stays consistent.
- initPrevalidated is safe: readArrayFromMeta validates every array.
- setColumnByName keeps first-match semantics for duplicate names (getOrPut keeps the first).
- Pairwise concat is sound: every type path handles left.offset symmetrically, the odd trailing ref keeps its order, the result is always fresh.
- Geometric growth: realloc keeps the 64-byte alignment; the empty static storage is never freed.
- Zero-copy: canReuseBodySlice handles alignment; non-owning sources are copied.
- Compat: the three build.zig helpers, CI matrix, README/CONTRIBUTING and zon all agree.
- Over-engineering: nothing to delete.

Verdict:
- Mergeable as-is: no blockers, both compilers pass the full suite.
- Before merge, do findings 1 and 2 (a one-line rule change plus one test) so the trust-boundary claim in the commit message holds.
- Finding 3 is a one-condition change; worth doing in the same commit.
- The nits can follow.
